lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation
lessonRef.title: Performance task planning: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows how to justify a modelling choice.

items.prompt: Mean 100, sd 15. What percentage lies between 70 and 130?

steps: That is 100 ± 30, which is two standard deviations.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Decide what the quantities are before you compute anything.

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.

items.prompt: A random sample of 625 people gives a sample proportion of 42%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 13 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 1.3% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 1.3% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Plan in writing: what you will model, why that model, and how you will check it.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 162 and standard deviation 5. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 152 and 172?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A random sample of 2500 people gives a sample proportion of 27%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
